2	\section{Analysis: Mechanisms of Phase-Modulated Severity}
3	\label{sec:analysis}
4	
5	The results in \S\ref{sec:results} reveal a striking asymmetry: importance-based eviction exhibits $69$--$274{\times}$ severity amplification in low-sparsity phases (Table~\ref{tab:main-results}), while random eviction remains flat at ${\sim}1{\times}$ across all phases. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; G=69,103,222,274
6	Why is compound severity phase-modulated for one strategy but not the other? We identify two mechanisms. \emph{Discrimination collapse}---a systematic reduction in the discriminative power of KV importance scores under head pruning---is the primary mechanism, robustly observed across both models and all tested conditions. A secondary \emph{entropy redistribution} pattern is consistent for DeepSeek but only partially replicates on Qwen, indicating model-dependent modulation.
7	
8	\subsection{Discrimination Collapse Under Head Pruning}
9	\label{sec:discrimination-collapse}
10	
11	The KV importance score (Eq.~\ref{eq:kv-importance}) aggregates attention mass across surviving heads. When head pruning reduces the number of contributing heads, the cumulative importance distribution becomes more uniform: the gap between highly-attended and rarely-attended positions shrinks. We quantify this effect through two complementary metrics applied to the per-position importance distribution.
12	
13	The \textbf{Gini coefficient} measures inequality in the importance distribution ($\mathrm{Gini}{=}0$: perfectly uniform; $\mathrm{Gini}{=}1$: maximally concentrated). The \textbf{coefficient of variation} (CV) captures relative dispersion. A decrease in either metric after pruning indicates reduced discriminative power.
14	
15	We observe discrimination collapse across both models in all tested conditions (Table~\ref{tab:discrimination-metrics}). Under importance-based eviction, the Gini delta is negative at every sparsity level for both DeepSeek ($-0.030$ to $-0.081$) and Qwen ($-0.010$ to $-0.020$), with magnitude scaling monotonically with sparsity in DeepSeek. % exp_id: c4_entropy_deepseek, c4_entropy_qwen
16	The CV delta is likewise negative in all 8 importance-based conditions, ranging from $-0.56$ to $-1.66$ (DeepSeek) and $-0.05$ to $-1.49$ (Qwen). The same pattern holds under random eviction (DeepSeek: $-0.031$ to $-0.073$; Qwen: $-0.019$ to $-0.045$), confirming that discrimination collapse is a consequence of head pruning \emph{per se}, not of the eviction strategy.
17	
18	\begin{table}[t]
19	\centering
20	\caption{Discrimination collapse under importance-based eviction. $\Delta\mathrm{Gini}$ and $\Delta\mathrm{CV}$ are post-pruning minus baseline; negative values indicate reduced discriminative power. All 8 conditions show consistent negative deltas across both models.}
21	\label{tab:discrimination-metrics}
22	\small
23	\begin{tabular}{llrr}
24	\toprule
25	Model & $s$ & $\Delta\mathrm{Gini}$ & $\Delta\mathrm{CV}$ \\
26	\midrule
27	DeepSeek & $0.15$ & $-0.030$ & $-0.56$ \\
28	DeepSeek & $0.20$ & $-0.040$ & $-0.77$ \\
29	DeepSeek & $0.25$ & $-0.065$ & $-1.29$ \\
30	DeepSeek & $0.30$ & $-0.081$ & $-1.66$ \\
31	\midrule
32	Qwen & $0.15$ & $-0.010$ & $-0.05$ \\
33	Qwen & $0.20$ & $-0.012$ & $-0.21$ \\
34	Qwen & $0.25$ & $-0.010$ & $-1.49$ \\
35	Qwen & $0.30$ & $-0.020$ & $-1.14$ \\
36	\bottomrule
37	\end{tabular}
38	\end{table}
39	
40	This cross-model consistency establishes discrimination collapse as a robust consequence of compound sparsity. When importance scores lose discriminative power, thresholding the bottom-$s$ fraction becomes noise-sensitive: small perturbations change which positions cross the eviction boundary. In the limit of perfectly uniform scores, importance-based eviction degenerates into an arbitrary selection functionally equivalent to biased random eviction. The severity inversion observed in \S\ref{sec:crossover} is thus an emergent consequence of the interaction between head pruning and importance scoring conditioned on the phase-dependent attention structure.
41	
42	Random eviction is immune to this mechanism: its decisions are independent of importance score quality. This explains the flat severity gradient ($G \approx 1$) observed under random eviction at all sparsity levels.
43	
44	\subsection{Entropy Redistribution: Consistent in DeepSeek, Partial in Qwen}
45	\label{sec:entropy-redistribution}
46	
47	Beyond discrimination collapse, we examine whether head pruning also redistributes the attention entropy of surviving heads. We measure the mean attention entropy per head:
48	\begin{equation}
49	    \mathcal{H}_i^{(h)} = -\sum_{j=1}^{T} a_{ij}^{(h)} \log a_{ij}^{(h)}
50	    \label{eq:attn-entropy}
51	\end{equation}
52	and compute $\Delta\mathcal{H}$ as the change from baseline (no pruning) to the pruned condition.
53	
54	For DeepSeek under importance-based eviction, the entropy delta is consistently negative across all four sparsity levels ($\Delta\mathcal{H} \in [-0.040, -0.047]$; Table~\ref{tab:entropy-deltas}), with the effect stable across reasoning phases. % exp_id: c4_entropy_deepseek
55	This is consistent with importance-based eviction systematically selecting heads whose removal concentrates attention in the surviving heads, reinforcing the discrimination collapse documented above.
56	
57	For Qwen, the entropy pattern only partially replicates. The delta is negative at $s{=}0.15$ ($\Delta\mathcal{H} = -0.073$) and $s{=}0.20$ ($-0.076$), consistent with DeepSeek. However, at $s{=}0.25$, the delta reverses to $+0.045$, with 22 of 30 problems showing positive entropy change. At $s{=}0.30$, the delta is near zero ($-0.007$). % exp_id: c4_entropy_qwen
58	
59	The $s{=}0.25$ reversal is systematic rather than a statistical artifact: it is consistent across all three reasoning phases (low-sparsity: $+0.042$, mid-sparsity: $+0.034$, high-sparsity: $+0.017$). The mid-sparsity phase contains fewer segments (median~26), which reduces statistical power for that phase; however, the reversal is equally present in the low-sparsity phase with substantially more segments, so mid-phase power limitations are a confound but do not account for the full pattern. We interpret this as a genuine model-specific difference, possibly arising from distinct head specialization patterns: Qwen's instruction tuning (vs.\ DeepSeek's distillation-based training) may produce head configurations where removing 25\% of heads triggers compensatory broadening rather than concentration.
60

62	\centering
63	\caption{Attention entropy deltas ($\Delta\mathcal{H}$) under importance-based eviction. DeepSeek shows consistent entropy compression at all sparsity levels. Qwen partially replicates: negative at $s{\leq}0.20$, reversed at $s{=}0.25$, near-zero at $s{=}0.30$.}
64	\label{tab:entropy-deltas}
65	\small
66	\begin{tabular}{llr}

68	Model & $s$ & $\Delta\mathcal{H}$ \\
69	\midrule
70	DeepSeek & $0.15$ & $-0.040$ \\
71	DeepSeek & $0.20$ & $-0.047$ \\
72	DeepSeek & $0.25$ & $-0.045$ \\
73	DeepSeek & $0.30$ & $-0.044$ \\
74	\midrule

76	Qwen & $0.20$ & $-0.076$ \\

82	
83	The partial replication of entropy redistribution, combined with the full replication of discrimination collapse, suggests a two-level mechanistic picture: head pruning universally degrades the discriminative power of importance scores (as measured by Gini and CV), while the specific direction of entropy redistribution depends on model-specific head specialization patterns. Discrimination collapse is sufficient on its own to explain the emergent phase-strategy interaction; entropy redistribution, where it co-occurs, may amplify the effect.
84	
85	\subsection{Implications for Compound Sparsity}
86	\label{sec:analysis-implications}
87	
88	The discrimination collapse mechanism suggests several broader conclusions.
89	
90	\paragraph{Architecture generality.} Discrimination collapse depends on two properties: (i)~attention-mass-based importance scoring for KV eviction, and (ii)~a sufficient number of pruned heads to degrade the importance distribution. Both are shared by the major KV cache compression methods---H$_2$O \cite{h2o2024}, SnapKV \cite{snapkv2024}, PyramidKV \cite{pyramidkv2024}---and by any autoregressive transformer producing extended reasoning traces. The cross-model consistency of the Gini and CV evidence (Table~\ref{tab:discrimination-metrics}) supports this generality. The entropy redistribution component, while consistent in DeepSeek, appears model-dependent; the full mechanism may thus manifest differently across architectures.
91	
92	\paragraph{Testable prediction.} Any importance metric derived from attention mass should exhibit discrimination collapse under head pruning, with the severity gradient scaling with the pruning-induced Gini decrease. Metrics that derive importance from sources independent of attention---such as activation magnitude or gradient-based saliency---would not be subject to the same collapse and should produce flatter severity gradients.
93	
94	\paragraph{Reframing compound severity.} The flat random baseline ($G \approx 1$) demonstrates that phase-modulated severity amplification is not an inherent cost of compound sparsity \emph{per se}. Rather, it is an emergent phase-strategy interaction---the consequence of applying a discrimination-sensitive eviction strategy in a regime where head pruning systematically degrades that discrimination. A phase-aware sparsity controller could, in principle, mitigate this interaction by adjusting the eviction budget or strategy per phase.

2	\section{Results}
3	\label{sec:results}
4	
5	We present our empirical findings in five parts: strategy-dependent compound severity (\S\ref{sec:strategy-severity}), phase-modulated amplification (\S\ref{sec:phase-amplification}), the phase-strategy crossover (\S\ref{sec:crossover}), cross-model replication (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}), and statistical validation (\S\ref{sec:stat-validation}).
6	
7	
8	\subsection{Experimental Overview}
9	\label{sec:exp-overview}
10	
11	We evaluate compound sparsity on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B using a 50-problem stratified subset of MATH-500 (\S\ref{sec:dataset}). For each problem, we measure perplexity under four conditions---dense, attention-only pruning, KV-only eviction, and compound (both)---at sparsity levels $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$. We compare importance-based and random eviction strategies (\S\ref{sec:sparsity-config}), and segment each generated sequence into high-, mid-, and low-sparsity reasoning phases via quantile-based attention sparsity partitioning (\S\ref{sec:phase-seg}). The interaction index (II, Eq.~\ref{eq:ii}) quantifies compound super-additivity, and the severity gradient ($G$, Eq.~\ref{eq:gradient}) captures phase-dependent amplification.
12	Models are evaluated in \texttt{bfloat16} precision (\S\ref{sec:experimental-setup}). Full experimental details appear therein.
13	
14	
15	\subsection{Strategy-Dependent Severity (C1)}

Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as approximately constant across the generation process.
We show that this assumption is wrong: compound sparsity severity is an emergent phase-strategy interaction that varies by over an order of magnitude across reasoning phases.

We evaluate compound sparsity on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (both Qwen2 architecture, 7B parameters) using 50 MATH-500 problems, measuring the Interaction Index---a super-additivity metric---across quantile-segmented reasoning phases at sparsity levels $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Long-context language models place acute pressure on the key--value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length and dominates inference memory at scale \cite{kwon2023vllm, pope2023efficiently}.
5	Two complementary responses have emerged: \emph{attention head pruning}, which removes structurally redundant heads \cite{voita2019heads, michel2019sixteen}, and \emph{KV cache eviction}, which discards low-importance token positions from the cache \cite{snapkv-neurips2024, adakv-neurips2025}.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Long-context language models place acute pressure on the key--value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length and dominates inference memory at scale \cite{kwon2023vllm, pope2023efficiently}.
Two complementary responses have emerged: \emph{attention head pruning}, which removes structurally redundant heads \cite{voita2019heads, michel2019sixteen}, and \emph{KV cache eviction}, which discards low-importance token positions from the cache \cite{snapkv-neurips2024, adakv-neurips2025}.
Deploying both simultaneously---\emph{compound sparsity}---is attractive because the compression gains multiply, but the resulting quality degradation can be super-additive: the joint loss exceeds the sum of individual losses \cite{spark-aaai2026, slim-icml2025}.

Prior work has characterized compound interaction as a property of the sparsity level---higher sparsity yields more interaction---but treats the interaction magnitude as roughly constant across the generation process \cite{spark-aaai2026, unicomp-2026}.
This assumption is problematic for reasoning-capable models, whose generations are structurally heterogeneous: a single chain-of-thought trace alternates between phases of broadly distributed attention (exploratory reasoning) and phases of sharply concentrated attention (structured computation) \cite{thinkv-iclr2026, decision-repr-transition-2026}.
If compound interaction severity varies across these phases, then a uniform sparsity budget---the standard deployment practice---may be safe in one phase yet destructive in another.

We investigate whether compound sparsity severity is modulated by reasoning phase and eviction strategy.
Our central finding is that it is, and strongly so: under importance-based KV cache eviction, the Interaction Index---a measure of super-additive compound degradation---is concentrated in the low-sparsity phase (where attention distributes broadly) and largely absent in the high-sparsity phase (where attention is focused).
This \emph{severity gradient} grows monotonically with the sparsity budget: on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the median phase difference in Interaction Index rises from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$, with paired effect sizes increasing from $d{=}0.44$ (small) to $d{=}0.80$ (large); Bonferroni-corrected permutation tests confirm significance at all four sparsity levels on this model ($p < 0.005$).
The pattern replicates at $s \geq 0.20$ on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($d \geq 0.55$) with attenuated absolute magnitude, though the effect at $s{=}0.15$ is marginal ($d{=}0.28$, bootstrap CI includes zero).
Critically, random eviction produces no such gradient: 7/8 conditions across both models fail to exhibit a significant phase difference (the single exception---Qwen $s{=}0.30$---has negligible effect size, $d{=}{-}0.04$), confirming that the severity gradient is an emergent property of the interaction between importance scoring and phase-dependent attention structure, not an artifact of compound sparsity per se.

We propose \emph{entropy-discrimination collapse} as an explanatory mechanism.
Head pruning forces surviving heads to redistribute attention mass, increasing attention entropy.
In low-sparsity phases, where attention is already broadly distributed, this redistribution flattens the cumulative importance scores used for KV eviction, degrading their discriminative power.
Importance-based eviction then degenerates into a biased pseudo-random process that can inadvertently remove critical positions---amplifying compound severity.
In high-sparsity phases, attention concentration is preserved after pruning, importance scores remain discriminative, and eviction remains well-targeted.
Random eviction is immune to this mechanism because its decisions are independent of attention patterns.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We identify a \textbf{phase--strategy interaction} in compound sparsity: importance-based eviction exhibits a severity gradient across reasoning phases that is absent under random eviction (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
    \item We show that this severity gradient \textbf{increases monotonically with sparsity} and replicate the finding at moderate-to-high sparsity ($s \geq 0.20$) across two models with different training regimes (distillation vs.\ instruction tuning), establishing robustness within the Qwen2 architecture family (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
    \item We propose \textbf{entropy-discrimination collapse} as a mechanistic explanation, linking head pruning to the degradation of importance-score discriminability in a phase-dependent manner (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{enumerate}

These findings challenge the implicit assumption that compound interaction magnitude is phase-invariant, and suggest that sparsity budgets should be allocated in a phase-aware manner---tightening compression during low-sparsity reasoning phases where compound interaction is most severe.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: \S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on compound compression, KV cache eviction, and phase-aware inference; \S\ref{sec:background} formalizes compound sparsity and introduces the Interaction Index; \S\ref{sec:experimental-setup} describes our experimental setup; \S\ref{sec:experiments} presents the main results; \S\ref{sec:analysis} analyzes the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism; and \S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications and limitations.

5	
6	Our contributions, mapped to confirmed claims, are:
7	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
8	    \item \textbf{Strategy dependence (C1).} Compound severity depends qualitatively on the eviction strategy: importance-based eviction produces phase-modulated interaction (median phase difference $0.39$--$14.59$), while random eviction shows no significant phase modulation in 7/8 conditions (the sole exception---Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$, $d{=}{-}0.04$---has negligible effect size).

10	    \item \textbf{Phase modulation (C2).} Under importance-based eviction, the median Interaction Index difference between low- and high-sparsity phases increases monotonically with sparsity (Bonferroni-corrected $p < 0.005$ at all four levels), with paired effect sizes growing from $d{=}0.44$ (small) to $d{=}0.80$ (large).
11	
12	    \item \textbf{Phase-strategy crossover (C3).} At $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction simultaneously outperforms random in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) and underperforms in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$)---a qualitative reversal in strategy ranking.
13	
14	    \item \textbf{Sub-exponential growth (C6).} The severity gradient grows with sparsity but at a decelerating rate, suggesting a natural ceiling on phase-dependent amplification.
15

19	\end{enumerate}

4	\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
5	One might argue that the qualitative direction of our findings is intuitive: in low-sparsity phases, attention distributes broadly across many tokens, so importance scores carry less discriminative signal, and importance-based eviction should degrade.
6	We do not dispute this intuition.
7	The surprise lies in the quantitative structure of the interaction, which is not predictable from first principles alone.
8	
9	First, the \emph{magnitude} of the severity gradient---$69$--$274{\times}$ amplification across sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results})---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; source: experiment_summary_table.json; G=low/high=69,103,222,274.
10	A reviewer expecting a $2$--$3\times$ effect would find two-orders-of-magnitude amplification difficult to anticipate without measurement.
11	Second, the gradient is \emph{phase-specific}: compound interaction concentrates in low-sparsity phases while high-sparsity phases exhibit near-zero compound interaction ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 0.06$ at $s \leq 0.30$; at $s = 0.35$, high-phase II rises to 0.105, indicating the onset of compound interaction even in high-sparsity phases at extreme pruning rates). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; high-phase medians: 0.006, 0.015, 0.032, 0.053

13	Third, and most strikingly, a \emph{crossover} emerges: at $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction \emph{outperforms} random eviction in high-sparsity phases (median severity $0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet \emph{underperforms} in low-sparsity phases ($7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$---a ${>}5{\times}$ severity inflation relative to random). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s025, bf16_ds_rand_s025; source: experiment_summary_table.json; high: imp=0.032, rand=0.818; low: imp=7.196, rand=1.363

17	
18	\paragraph{Random masking as a falsification control.}
19	The random eviction baseline provides a decisive test against the ``trivially expected'' objection.
20	If compound severity amplification were an inherent property of applying two compression methods jointly---rather than an emergent phase-strategy interaction---random eviction should exhibit a comparable phase gradient.

22	The absence of a phase gradient under random masking isolates the amplification as strategy-specific: it arises from the interaction between importance-based eviction and phase structure, not from compound sparsity per se.
23

25	The phase-strategy interaction replicates across both models with perfect ordinal agreement: the Spearman rank correlation of Cohen's $d$ effect sizes across sparsity levels is $\rho{=}1.0$, and a gradient permutation test confirms this monotonic co-escalation ($p{=}0.043$). % exp_id: cross_model_correlation; Spearman rho=1.0, gradient_perm p=0.043

27

29	Qwen's median severity differences ($0.039 \to 0.235 \to 1.268 \to 2.943$) are approximately one-fifth of DeepSeek's ($0.39 \to 1.48 \to 7.16 \to 14.59$), and the onset threshold differs: DeepSeek's gradient is significant from $s{=}0.15$ (Cohen's $d{=}0.442$), while Qwen's becomes clearly significant only at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d{=}0.549$; $s{=}0.15$ is borderline at $d{=}0.281$ with CI crossing zero). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json (ds: 0.442,0.520,0.683,0.803), cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json (qw: 0.281,0.549,0.889,1.022).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
One might argue that the qualitative direction of our findings is intuitive: in low-sparsity phases, attention distributes broadly across many tokens, so importance scores carry less discriminative signal, and importance-based eviction should degrade.
We do not dispute this intuition.
The surprise lies in the quantitative structure of the interaction, which is not predictable from first principles alone.

First, the \emph{magnitude} of the severity gradient---$69$--$274{\times}$ amplification across sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results})---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; source: experiment_summary_table.json; G=low/high=69,103,222,274.
A reviewer expecting a $2$--$3\times$ effect would find two-orders-of-magnitude amplification difficult to anticipate without measurement.
Second, the gradient is \emph{phase-specific}: compound interaction concentrates in low-sparsity phases while high-sparsity phases exhibit near-zero compound interaction ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 0.06$ at $s \leq 0.30$; at $s = 0.35$, high-phase II rises to 0.105, indicating the onset of compound interaction even in high-sparsity phases at extreme pruning rates). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; high-phase medians: 0.006, 0.015, 0.032, 0.053
This asymmetry means that importance-based eviction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner.
Third, and most strikingly, a \emph{crossover} emerges: at $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction \emph{outperforms} random eviction in high-sparsity phases (median severity $0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet \emph{underperforms} in low-sparsity phases ($7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$---a ${>}5{\times}$ severity inflation relative to random). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s025, bf16_ds_rand_s025; source: experiment_summary_table.json; high: imp=0.032, rand=0.818; low: imp=7.196, rand=1.363
The same strategy reverses direction across phases---a phenomenon that cannot be derived from the observation that ``importance scores are noisier when attention is diffuse.''
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "The qualitative direction is trivially expected from attention entropy arguments."
% REBUTTAL: (1) Qualitative direction ≠ quantitative structure: 69-274× amplification is two orders of magnitude, not marginal. (2) Phase-specific concentration + crossover cannot be predicted from single-layer entropy reasoning. (3) Random eviction's flat profile (~1×) shows the amplification is strategy-specific, not an inherent property of compound sparsity.

\paragraph{Random masking as a falsification control.}
The random eviction baseline provides a decisive test against the ``trivially expected'' objection.
If compound severity amplification were an inherent property of applying two compression methods jointly---rather than an emergent phase-strategy interaction---random eviction should exhibit a comparable phase gradient.
It does not: random eviction fails seven of eight paired permutation tests across both models (7/8 FAIL); the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) exhibits negligible effect size ($d{=}{-}0.04$), producing no practically meaningful phase-modulated severity. % exp_id: bf16_ds_rand_s015..s030, bf16_qw_rand_s015..s030; verdict: 7/8 FAIL, 1 PASS (qw_rand_s030 p=0.012 d=-0.035 negligible)
The absence of a phase gradient under random masking isolates the amplification as strategy-specific: it arises from the interaction between importance-based eviction and phase structure, not from compound sparsity per se.

\paragraph{Cross-model replication and magnitude asymmetry.}
The phase-strategy interaction replicates across both models with perfect ordinal agreement: the Spearman rank correlation of Cohen's $d$ effect sizes across sparsity levels is $\rho{=}1.0$, and a gradient permutation test confirms this monotonic co-escalation ($p{=}0.043$). % exp_id: cross_model_correlation; Spearman rho=1.0, gradient_perm p=0.043
All eight paired Wilcoxon tests (4 sparsity levels $\times$ 2 models) reject $H_0$, confirming the pattern is not an artifact of a single model's weight structure.

The \emph{magnitude} of the effect, however, differs substantially.
Qwen's median severity differences ($0.039 \to 0.235 \to 1.268 \to 2.943$) are approximately one-fifth of DeepSeek's ($0.39 \to 1.48 \to 7.16 \to 14.59$), and the onset threshold differs: DeepSeek's gradient is significant from $s{=}0.15$ (Cohen's $d{=}0.442$), while Qwen's becomes clearly significant only at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d{=}0.549$; $s{=}0.15$ is borderline at $d{=}0.281$ with CI crossing zero). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json (ds: 0.442,0.520,0.683,0.803), cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json (qw: 0.281,0.549,0.889,1.022).
The two models share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture but differ in training: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is distilled from a larger reasoning model, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct undergoes standard instruction tuning.
We conjecture that distillation amplifies the phase-strategy interaction by producing sharper internal phase transitions---a hypothesis testable by comparing distilled and non-distilled variants at matched scale.

\paragraph{Mechanistic evidence: discrimination collapse as the robust signal.}
The entropy-discrimination collapse hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) receives partial cross-model support.
The discrimination components---Gini coefficient reduction and coefficient-of-variation compression under compound sparsity---are directionally consistent across both models, confirming that importance-based eviction loses discriminative power in low-sparsity phases regardless of training procedure.
However, the entropy component is model-dependent: DeepSeek exhibits consistent negative entropy shifts (attention concentrates further under head pruning), while Qwen shows a sign reversal at $s{=}0.25$ ($\Delta H {=} {+}0.045$) and near-zero shift at $s{=}0.30$ ($\Delta H {=} {-}0.007$). % exp_id: mechanism_entropy_qwen; s025: +0.045, s030: -0.007
This divergence suggests that discrimination collapse---not entropy redistribution---is the primary driver of the phase-strategy interaction, with entropy behavior being a model-dependent secondary effect.

Our findings suggest that the standard practice of applying a uniform compression budget across all inference steps is suboptimal for reasoning models.
Compound severity is not distributed evenly: it concentrates in low-sparsity phases, where the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) renders importance-based eviction unreliable.
A deployment pipeline that allocates the same sparsity level $s$ to every token position implicitly accepts order-of-magnitude severity penalties during the exploratory reasoning stages that happen to fall in the low-sparsity regime.

The severity gradient $G$ reported in \S\ref{sec:phase-amplification} provides a natural signal for such allocation: phases with $G \gg 1$ receive a reduced sparsity budget, while phases with $G \leq 1$ tolerate aggressive compression with minimal quality loss.

The phase-aware allocation principle above points toward a concrete system design: a \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity statistics in real time and dynamically adjusts the compound sparsity budget per reasoning phase.
The controller would route each generation step through a low-overhead phase classifier (\S\ref{sec:phase-seg}), then apply a phase-specific sparsity configuration derived from the severity gradient.

% REBUTTAL: Correct—we explicitly state this is cross-model (different training: distillation vs instruction tuning), not cross-architecture. The two models isolate the training variable while controlling architecture. Cross-architecture validation (LLaMA, Mistral) is acknowledged as future work.

import json
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from pathlib import Path

BASE = Path("/root/autodl-tmp/pacs")
OUTPUT = BASE / "analysis_output" / "rebootstrap_b10000_results.json"

B = 10000
SEED = 42

EXPERIMENTS = {
    "bf16_ds_imp_s015": {"path": "profiling_output_bf16_ds_imp_s015", "level": "0.15", "model": "DeepSeek"},
    "bf16_ds_imp_s020": {"path": "profiling_output_bf16_ds_imp_s020", "level": "0.2",  "model": "DeepSeek"},

    "bf16_qw_imp_s030": {"path": "profiling_output_bf16_qw_imp_s030", "level": "0.3",  "model": "Qwen"},
}


def load_paired(path, level):
    with open(path) as f:
        data = json.load(f)
    old_B = data["config"].get("n_bootstrap", "unknown")
    ppi = data["per_problem_ii"][level]
    ii_high, ii_low = [], []
    for p in ppi:
        h, l = p.get("ii_high"), p.get("ii_low")
        if h is not None and l is not None:
            ii_high.append(h)
            ii_low.append(l)
    return np.array(ii_high), np.array(ii_low), old_B


def permutation_test(ii_high, ii_low, B=10000, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    obs = np.median(ii_low) - np.median(ii_high)
    pooled = np.concatenate([ii_high, ii_low])
    n_h = len(ii_high)
    count = 0
    for _ in range(B):
        rng.shuffle(pooled)
        d = np.median(pooled[n_h:]) - np.median(pooled[:n_h])
        if abs(d) >= abs(obs):
            count += 1
    return round(count / B, 6)


def bootstrap_ci(ii_high, ii_low, B=10000, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    n = min(len(ii_high), len(ii_low))
    diffs = np.empty(B)
    for i in range(B):
        idx_h = rng.randint(0, len(ii_high), size=n)
        idx_l = rng.randint(0, len(ii_low), size=n)
        diffs[i] = np.median(ii_low[idx_l]) - np.median(ii_high[idx_h])
    return round(float(np.percentile(diffs, 2.5)), 6), round(float(np.percentile(diffs, 97.5)), 6)


def cohens_d(ii_high, ii_low):
    n1, n2 = len(ii_low), len(ii_high)
    s1, s2 = np.std(ii_low, ddof=1), np.std(ii_high, ddof=1)
    pooled_std = np.sqrt(((n1-1)*s1**2 + (n2-1)*s2**2) / (n1+n2-2))
    return round(float((np.mean(ii_low) - np.mean(ii_high)) / pooled_std), 6) if pooled_std > 0 else 0.0


def main():
    results = {}
    print(f"{'Experiment':<22} {'Old B':<8} {'median_diff':<14} {'perm_p':<10} {'cohen_d':<10} {'CI_low':<12} {'CI_high':<12} {'wilcox_p':<12}")
    print("-" * 110)

    for exp_id, cfg in EXPERIMENTS.items():
        fpath = BASE / cfg["path"] / "profiling_results.json"
        if not fpath.exists():
            print(f"{exp_id:<22} NOT FOUND")
            continue

        ii_high, ii_low, old_B = load_paired(str(fpath), cfg["level"])
        n_paired = len(ii_high)

        med_diff = round(float(np.median(ii_low) - np.median(ii_high)), 6)
        perm_p = permutation_test(ii_high, ii_low, B=B, seed=SEED)
        ci_lo, ci_hi = bootstrap_ci(ii_high, ii_low, B=B, seed=SEED)
        cd = cohens_d(ii_high, ii_low)

        n = min(len(ii_high), len(ii_low))
        wt = stats.wilcoxon(ii_low[:n], ii_high[:n], alternative='two-sided')
        wilcox_p = round(float(wt.pvalue), 6)

        print(f"{exp_id:<22} {old_B:<8} {med_diff:<14.6f} {perm_p:<10.4f} {cd:<10.4f} {ci_lo:<12.6f} {ci_hi:<12.6f} {wilcox_p:<12.6f}")

            "old_n_bootstrap": old_B,
            "new_n_bootstrap": B,
            "n_paired": n_paired,
            "median_diff": med_diff,
            "permutation_p": perm_p,
            "cohens_d": cd,
            "bootstrap_ci_95": [ci_lo, ci_hi],
            "wilcoxon_p": wilcox_p,
        }

    OUTPUT.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with open(OUTPUT, "w") as f:
        json.dump(results, f, indent=2)
    print(f"\nResults saved to {OUTPUT}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
